claims.evidence: NHS Inform: nerve damage can dull feeling so daily checks matter; Diabetes UK: check every day and annual foot check.
NHS Inform: nerve damage can dull feeling, some people have no symptoms at all.
Diabetes UK: check feet every day, ideally when putting socks on in the morning and before bed.
Diabetes UK: foot check is part of the yearly diabetes review and free on the NHS.
NHFT: hot, red, swollen foot, wound or infection signs - contact GP, podiatrist or diabetic foot team right away; NHS Inform similar.
NHS Inform: high glucose for a long time can cause nerve damage (neuropathy) in the feet, dulling feeling.
Retrieved text only says circulation to the feet can be affected (NHS Inform) and Lanarkshire mentions reduced circulation; 'narrow the arteries' and 'slows healing' not stated in what was retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Diabetes can also affect the circulation to the feet.

claims.evidence: Diabetes UK says if feeling is lost you may not notice an injury; 'will not know' is stronger than the source.
claims.newSentence: Diabetes UK says that if feeling has been lost, a person may not notice an injury to the foot.

claims.evidence: Burning or pins and needles not found in retrieved text.
NHS Inform: smoking can affect circulation to the feet; NHFT: smoking damages circulation.
Diabetes UK: check when putting socks on in the morning and before bed.
NHFT: look at tops, soles, heels, between toes; NHS Inform: use a mirror or get help from someone.
NHS Inform: cuts, breaks in skin, hard skin; NHFT: redness, swelling, blisters, wounds, colour changes.
NHFT: wash daily in warm water, dry thoroughly especially between toes, moisturise dry skin.
Sources advise moisturising but avoiding between the toes; the reason ('can cause problems') and Diabetes UK attribution not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: NHS sources describe moisturising dry skin but avoiding the gaps between the toes.

claims.evidence: Diabetes UK says avoid shoes and socks that are too tight, too loose or rub; 'even if comfortable' not found.
claims.newSentence: Diabetes UK says shoes and socks that are too tight, too loose or that rub can cause problems.

claims.evidence: Diabetes UK advises checking inside and outside shoes before wearing; sharp-object example not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: It advises checking inside and outside footwear before putting it on.

claims.evidence: Sources recommend changing socks daily, natural fibres like cotton or wool, no thick seams or holes; 'darns' and exact attribution to Diabetes UK/NHS Scotland not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: UK sources describe changing socks daily and choosing natural fibres such as cotton or wool, without holes or thick seams.

claims.evidence: Wrong attribution: Diabetes UK says to cut nails carefully, not too short; it is NHS Scotland/NHFT that say high-risk people should not cut toenails unless a podiatrist advises.
claims.newSentence: NHS sources say people at high risk should not cut their own toenails unless a podiatrist advises it.

claims.evidence: Diabetes UK: foot check is part of the annual review and free on the NHS.
Retrieved: clinician checks blood flow (pulses/doppler) and podiatrist checks circulation and sensation; footwear check not found.
claims.newSentence: The check looks at sensation and at blood flow in the feet.

claims.evidence: Diabetes UK describes low, moderate and high categories; Lanarkshire says low, moderate or high risk of problems (not 'medium', not specifically ulcer).
claims.newSentence: The result places a person in a low, moderate or high risk category for foot problems.

claims.evidence: 12-24 months for NHS Lanarkshire could not be confirmed on re-check. Diabetes UK: low risk checks move to every other year; moderate usually keep yearly checks.
claims.newSentence: Diabetes UK says that people at low risk may move to a check every other year, while those at moderate risk usually keep having yearly checks.

claims.evidence: NICE NG19 'Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management' confirmed; a public version not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: NICE has a guideline on preventing and managing diabetic foot problems.

claims.evidence: NHS Inform: contact podiatrist/GP urgently for hot red swollen foot, new skin damage, change in shape, new pain; NHFT adds diabetic foot team, wound not healing.

NHFT lists signs of infection (redness, swelling, oozing, discharge, bad smell) for same-day help; NHS Inform says call 111 for fever, shivering, feeling unwell. 'Wound getting larger' and 'increasing warmth' not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: NHS sources describe seeking help the same day for signs of infection such as redness, swelling, oozing or a bad smell, and NHS Inform says to call NHS 111 for new foot problems with fever, shivering or feeling generally unwell.

claims.evidence: NHS Inform: phone 999 or go to A&E if foot changing colour (very pale or blue), especially with new numbness or pain.
NHS Inform: phone 111 if podiatrist or GP practice is closed.

notes: Search results were summaries, not full text. NHS Inform 111 is NHS 24 in Scotland; the site is UK-wide so consider noting local variation. Lanarkshire 12-24 month claim appeared in one summary and could not be reproduced; dropped. NHFT page is a trust blog, so 'NHS sources' wording is acceptable but not 'NHS says'.
